title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
dek: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.
why: A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.
who: Founders and investors interested in philosophy of science, interpretations of quantum mechanics, Keynes and Bloomsbury intellectual history; anyone looking for judgment frameworks of the ‘perspective rather than single answer’ kind.
skip: The podcast ads around 29:16 and the programme trailer at 42:50 can be skipped.

points.h: A glass of water has no final version
points.body: Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is that all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘ultimate glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

points.h: We have not yet digested quantum mechanics
points.body: Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is an enormous revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we do not yet truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of the observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

points.h: The deepest level of reality is not more objective
points.body: Rovelli turns it around: the most basic level of reality physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or the characters in James's play deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard; it simply has not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course very complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and putting a piece of each together into a new concept. The goal is not to arrive at a final perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain better understanding, better ways of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective is not the same as saying all perspectives are equal, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

points.h: Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
points.body: Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is ‘what is a good life’.

points.h: Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
points.body: Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, and a poet has to as well. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means’. She gives the example of poems on the Underground: before everyone was looking at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem, and that kind of engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

points.h: Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
points.body: James Graham says modern culture has fetishised ‘efficiency’ and stripped out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — ‘this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — and his reaction is ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read it’. He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

Rovelli uses the International Day of Peace on 21 September, and speeches by the UN Secretary-General and the Pope, to connect the argument about perspectives to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford immediately offers a counterexample: we also always need to pursue simplicity; if you embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day, you might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people how to argue.

points.h: Buying paintings for twenty thousand pounds in wartime
points.body: James Graham tells the most gripping piece of history in his play: during the First World War Britain had just gone from being a world creditor to a debtor, and Keynes, as a junior adviser at the Treasury, asked Treasury officials and the Permanent Secretary for £20,000 to go to Paris to buy paintings, because Edgar Degas's collection was coming up for auction. At the time all the money was flowing to armaments and the war. No one knows what he said at that meeting, so the playwright gets to write his words for him. Graham says the ‘absurdity’ of the case is precisely its power: if there was any money left over, what should be done is to buy a few paintings and put them in the National Gallery, because in the future it is both an asset on the government's balance sheet and an asset that lets the nation have beautiful things to look at after the war — ‘if peace is not about creating things that make people happy in the future, then what is it?’

points.h: Two men on a church roof watching for incendiaries
points.body: The opposition between Keynes and Hayek is written by Graham as the core of the play: Hayek represents the Adam Smith tradition of the ‘invisible hand’ — let it be, it will self-correct, and intervening with imperfect human hands is dangerous and reckless; Keynes represents the interventionist mixed economy of the postwar consensus from 1945 to 1979. The two did meet, and on one occasion during the Second World War both were on the roof of the chapel at King's College, Cambridge as fire watchers, entirely by chance, watching the Luftwaffe fly over looking for incendiaries. No one knows what they said that night, and Graham says this is a gift to a playwright, so he wrote their dialogue: Keynes says ‘Hayek, without imagination, how do we dream a new world’, and Hayek replies ‘You do the dreaming, Mr Keynes, I like to stay awake’.

quotes.text: So I think the main thesis of my book is that all these perspectives are all real, neither exhaust any other one, neither contradicts any other one, and there isn't an ultimate glass of water.
We haven't yet digested quantum mechanics.
It only means that the hope of getting to a final correct story about reality, it's an empty hope because I would say it's not something unreachable. It's something meaningless.

If we ask the question, what is the ultimate definition of good and bad? What is the ultimate morality, the ultimate ethics, the universal one? I think we are doing something morally wrong, ethically wrong.
And again, back to my people, the Bloomsbury's and Keynes, it's in the friction, it's in the difficulty, it's in the process that you discover meaning.
To which Hayek says, well, you feel free to dream, Mr. Keynes, I like being awake.
I think progress comes in the moment in which we realize that reality is more complicated than the way we see it.
